answer_short.case-1: Chinese graphite goes in, and graphite goes out to five US battery and car makers. Who owns the plant isn't in the registry.
answer_short.case-2: BTR's 100% ownership is on record. The first graphite arrived from BTR's own Indonesian plant in Aug 2026, and nothing has been exported yet.
answer_short.case-3: The Oman plant isn't in the data yet. Zhongke graphite reaches the US today through Malaysian cell plants.
answer_short.case-4: Korean-owned, with Chinese graphite inputs. It sells to the same US buyers as BTR Indonesia.
answer_short.case-5: No Chinese-owned anode maker is shipping to the US from five corridors. Putailai's Malaysian plant is still being built.
answer_short.case-6: Chinese anode graphite goes in and finished cells go out to US buyers, from a plant owned by China's EVE Energy.
answer_short.case-7: Gotion's Chinese plants ship cells, packs and graphite to its US sites, which its annual report says it wholly owns, though no US record shows it.
answer_short.case-8: A non-Chinese chain from Mozambique to Louisiana, but the same mine also supplies Chinese-owned plants.
answer_short.case-11: CATL's 100% ownership is on record, but EU-internal trade is invisible: only Chinese factory equipment shows up, and no battery materials.
answer_short.case-10: CATL's group owned Linergy until June 2026, when Japan's TDK bought it. Sayari still shows the old Chinese chain.
answer_short.case-9: Yes, but not via Morocco yet: BTR graphite reached Ford's Michigan plant from Indonesia in 2026, and BlueOval SK from China in 2025.
answer_short.case-12: Huayou's Indonesian nickel plant sends its output to Chinese refiners and traders. No nickel goes directly to the US, and the hop to US cathodes isn't joined by any record.

Chinese parent ownership of the transit.detected: Get the full shareholder chain to the ultimate owner, with percentages, and check each owner against the US prohibited-foreign-entity definitions.
Chinese parent ownership of the transit.suggested: Ownership rests on indirect evidence. Ask the supplier for a registry extract that names its shareholders.
Chinese parent ownership of the transit.not_visible: Ownership couldn't be confirmed. Ask for a registry extract and an ownership certification before relying on the supplier.
Chinese parent ownership of the transit.absent: No Chinese owner found. Keep a dated record of the ownership check and repeat it each year.

Same HS imported from China and exported.detected: The plant imports Chinese graphite and exports graphite to the US. Ask for lot-level origin certificates for the material you buy.
Same HS imported from China and exported.suggested: Inputs may include Chinese graphite. Ask what share of feedstock is Chinese-origin.
Same HS imported from China and exported.not_visible: Input origin couldn't be tested. Ask the supplier to list its graphite feedstock sources.
Same HS imported from China and exported.absent: No Chinese graphite inputs found in the data. Confirm with the supplier that this is still true.

Recent incorporation vs. first export da.detected: The company was set up shortly before exporting. Ask about its operating history and its real production capacity.
Recent incorporation vs. first export da.suggested: Check the incorporation date against first shipments.
Recent incorporation vs. first export da.not_visible: No incorporation date was available. Request the certificate of incorporation.
Recent incorporation vs. first export da.absent: Long operating history; no concern on this point.

Volume spike after a policy date.detected: Volumes changed after a policy date. Ask why, and whether the routing or product changed.
Volume spike after a policy date.not_visible: Not tested. Compare monthly volumes before and after July 2025 and March 2026.
Volume spike after a policy date.absent: No spike seen in the data.

Shared address or officer with a flagged.detected: The supplier shares an address or officer with a flagged company. Ask who the shared party is and what the relationship is.
Shared address or officer with a flagged.suggested: A possible shared officer or address. Confirm the relationship.
Shared address or officer with a flagged.absent: No shared address or officer with a flagged company found.

Entity-resolution fragmentation.detected: The supplier appears under several names. Agree with it the exact legal entity, registration number and address that should appear on your documents.
Entity-resolution fragmentation.suggested: Possible duplicate records. Confirm the legal entity.

Forced-labor / UFLPA sub-tier flags.detected: Sub-tier forced-labor flags appear. Request a supply-chain map to the mine or precursor level and check it against the UFLPA Entity List.
Forced-labor / UFLPA sub-tier flags.suggested: Possible sub-tier forced-labor exposure. Ask for a sub-tier supplier list.
